seo_title: Chupacabra: Puerto Rico's goat-sucker, the Texas dogs and what it really is
seo_desc: The chupacabra story from the 1995 Puerto Rico attacks to the hairless Texas carcasses. Who named it, what the DNA tests found, the movie link and the Moca vampire that came first.
summary: The goat-sucker blamed for draining livestock in 1995 Puerto Rico, which later turned into the hairless dogs of Texas.
body: In 1995 farmers in Puerto Rico started finding goats, sheep and chickens dead with small puncture wounds. A woman in Canóvanas described a spiny creature with big dark eyes walking on two legs, a radio comedian came up with the name chupacabras, and it took off from there.

As the reports spread into Mexico and Texas the chupacabra changed shape completely. In the US it's usually a hairless, grey, dog-like animal, and every one that's been tested has turned out to be a coyote, dog or fox with a bad case of mange.

p: The first attack people later tied to it happened in March 1995, when eight sheep were found dead in Puerto Rico, each with three puncture wounds in the chest and supposedly drained of blood. Then in August a woman named Madelyne Tolentino said she saw the creature in Canóvanas. Around the same time there were reports of up to 150 dead farm animals and pets in the area, and more than 200 reports on the island that year.

The name came from Silverio Pérez, a Puerto Rican comedian who was talking about the attacks on his radio show in San Juan. Chupacabras basically means goat-sucker (chupa for sucks, cabras for goats) and both chupacabras and chupacabra are used, so you're fine either way.

Funny enough, it wasn't the island's first livestock vampire. Back in 1975 a run of dead animals around the town of Moca got blamed on something people called el vampiro de Moca. We have a page on the [Moca vampire](/creatures/moca-vampire/) too.

Here's the part that changed how I look at the whole thing. Writer and investigator Benjamin Radford spent five years on the case for his 2011 book Tracking the Chupacabra, and he found that Tolentino's description lines up almost exactly with Sil, the alien creature from the 1995 sci-fi horror movie Species. She'd seen the movie before her sighting and even said herself that the creature in it looked like the chupacabra, spines on its back and all.

That doesn't mean she was lying. People mix up what they've seen on screen with what they saw in real life all the time. But since her description is the one that became THE chupacabra, it's a big deal.

sections.h: How it turned into a hairless dog
p: Once the story hit Mexico and the southern US the spiny, upright creature mostly disappeared and the reports turned into hairless, grey-blue dog-like animals with big teeth. That's the version you'll see in Texas.

In July 2004 a rancher near San Antonio shot what got called the Elmendorf Beast after it went after his livestock. DNA testing at UC Davis said coyote, with sarcoptic mange. In 2007 Phylis Canion in Cuero, Texas found a strange carcass after losing around 30 chickens over a few years, and had it preserved. Texas State University tested it and said coyote, and a second test at UC Davis said a coyote and Mexican wolf mix. Mange explained the bare, grey-blue skin. A year later a DeWitt County deputy filmed a hairless animal in Cuero alleys on his dash camera, and in 2010 one shot in Hood County, Texas turned out to be a coyote and dog mix with mange and parasites.

In 2010 University of Michigan biologist Barry O'Connor put it pretty simply. He said the US chupacabras were coyotes infected with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, which leaves them with little fur, thick skin and a bad smell. Sick animals like that are weak, so going after goats and chickens is easier for them than chasing down a rabbit. That explains the farm attacks too.

After Puerto Rico, dead-animal reports blamed on the chupacabra came from Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Central America, Colombia, Brazil, Argentina, Chile and as far away as Russia and the Philippines. In Calama, in northern Chile, around a hundred farm animals were reported dead in 2000, and the footprints and hair pointed to domestic dogs. In Argentina in 2002 the national animal health agency, SENASA, put a wave of cattle mutilations down to foxes and rats.

If you're into this kind of thing, the [cattle mutilation](/creatures/cattle-mutilation/) story has a lot in common with it, and so do the [Montauk monster](/creatures/montauk-monster/) and other mystery carcasses.

faq.a: Not as a new animal, no. Every hairless "chupacabra" from the US and Mexico that's been tested has been a coyote, dog, fox or a mix with severe mange. The original Puerto Rican description most likely came partly from the 1995 movie Species, according to Benjamin Radford's research.
Goat-sucker, from the Spanish chupar (to suck) and cabras (goats). The original Spanish is chupacabras and chupacabra is just the singular-sounding version that caught on.

faq.q: Where was the chupacabra first seen?
faq.a: Puerto Rico in 1995. The sighting that defined it was Madelyne Tolentino's in Canóvanas that August, after dead livestock started turning up earlier in the year.

faq.q: What does a chupacabra look like?
faq.a: Depends where you are. The Puerto Rican version is about the size of a small bear, stands on two legs and has big dark eyes and spines down its back. The Texas and Mexico version is a hairless, grey-blue, dog-like animal with big teeth.

faq.q: Why do chupacabras look like hairless dogs?
faq.a: Because they're mostly coyotes with sarcoptic mange. The mite makes the fur fall out and the skin go thick and grey, and the sick animals end up raiding farms because they're too weak to hunt normally.
Puerto Rican comedian Silverio Pérez is usually credited with coining it in 1995, while talking about the livestock attacks on his radio show in San Juan.
